notes:
Need to search first.I've written notes on 18 of the 21 verses. I found nothing usable for vv. 16, 17 and 18, so they're left out. My searches hit the tool's usage limit partway through, and several key pages wouldn't open at all, including the full Enduring Word chapter. Most of the notes below come from the page excerpts the search tool returned, not from complete pages.

For part 3 I found almost nothing. I got nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. The only Catholic voice is Cornelius à Lapide, a Jesuit commentator from 1614, quoted on a StudyLight page. The closest thing to modern scholarship is a verse-by-verse commentary on the Greek text at bible.org.

For part 2, I found no real Protestant disagreement by tradition. The open questions (the "sixth hour," whether Jesus was flogged once or twice, and who committed the "greater sin") split commentators individually, not along denominational lines. Where a source's tradition is clear, I've noted it.

---

**v. 1 (the flogging)**
- **Why Pilate did it:** Many commentators say the flogging was a compromise. Pilate hoped a lesser punishment would satisfy the crowd so he could let Jesus go. One commentator on the Bible Hub page calls it the move of a "weak and cynical nature" that only made the hatred bolder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-1.htm
- **Older commentators on the same page:** One adds that it was still unjust to flog a man Pilate himself found innocent. That writer also sees it as a picture of Christ bearing divine justice in his people's place, innocent and suffering for others' sins. The Geneva Study Bible note says worldly wisdom picks the lesser of two evils, but God curses that wisdom. Same URL.
- **The Expositor's Greek Testament:** It cites one scholar who thought the flogging was the first stage of crucifixion. It answers that in John it was a compromise, matching Luke 23:22 ("I will punish him and let him go"). Same URL.
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Pilate's repeated statements that Jesus was innocent show that Christ was sinless and was punished in place of the guilty. Pilate is a "trembling conscience": he declares Jesus innocent but punishes him anyway. Calvin adds that many "Pilates" still scourge Christ in his people and his teaching. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_john_volume_2/john_19_1-6.htm
- **One flogging or two?** Ligonier says John's flogging was probably the lighter beating (fustigatio). The severe one (verberatio), which Matthew and Mark place after the sentence, came later. This would explain the apparent difference between the Gospels. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/pilate-presents-jesus-to-crowd. Precept Austin sets out the same two-flogging order. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-19-commentary
- **Physical details:** Precept Austin describes the Roman whip (ox sinew woven with pieces of bone) and contrasts it with the milder Jewish method in the Mishnah (an early collection of Jewish law). https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-19-commentary. Barclay says few stayed conscious through it and some died, and he presents it as a sign of Jesus' physical courage. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dsb/john-19.html
- **Bible.org:** Pilate's officers did the flogging on his order. John's wording may echo Isaiah 50:6 ("I gave my back to those who strike"). https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-19

**vv. 2–3 (crown, robe, mock homage)**
- The soldiers covered his wounds with a robe in the royal colour and pressed a thorn wreath onto his head. The joke insulted the Jewish nation as well as the "King." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-1.htm
- Calvin says the mockery was meant to brand Jesus for claiming kingship, but the soldiers went further than the judge ordered. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_john_volume_2/john_19_1-6.htm
- Precept Austin notes the soldiers' scorn fell especially on the words "of the Jews." https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-19-commentary

**v. 4**
- Bible.org: the flogging seems to have happened inside the governor's headquarters (the Praetorium), and Pilate now goes outside again. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-19
- Precept Austin maps Pilate's movements in and out. The commentary on the Bible Hub page for v. 1 also says Pilate's back-and-forth shows his indecision. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-19-commentary ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-1.htm

**v. 5 ("Here is the man!")**
- **Mainly an appeal for pity:** Ellicott, Pulpit and Cambridge read it as "surely this is enough?" Cambridge points out that the Greek word means "wearing," as if the crown and robe were now his regular clothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-5.htm
- **Also a dismissal:** Clarke and Matthew Henry read it as "this is the dangerous rebel you fear?" Constable has Pilate showing a beaten, pathetic figure in place of the rival king they feared. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-5.html
- **Deeper meaning:** Sproul (Reformed, via Ligonier) sees Pilate unknowingly presenting the one perfect man, man as God intended him to be. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/pilate-presents-jesus-to-crowd. The Lutheran LCMS *Witness* article uses the verse to talk about the Word made flesh. https://witness.lcms.org/2026/why-we-memorize-scripture/
- Bible.org lists three possible senses: "here is the accused," a sneer, or a plea for pity. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-19

**v. 6**
- One commentator hears John's bare "Crucify, crucify!" as a wild roar. He reads Pilate's "you take him" as half anger, half sarcasm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-1.htm
- Bible.org thinks it unlikely Pilate was really giving permission. Frustration or sarcasm is more probable. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-19
- Calvin notes it is only the priests and officers shouting here, not the whole people. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_john_volume_2/john_19_1-6.htm
- A. T. Robertson (quoted at Precept Austin) calls Pilate's reasoning, giving up while declaring Jesus innocent, the strangest court ruling ever. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-19-commentary

**v. 7**
- **The real charge:** Enduring Word says this shows the leaders' true charge. They wanted him dead for claiming to be the unique Son of God, equal with God, not for claiming to be king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/ Chuck Smith makes the same point. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Jhn/Jhn_129.cfm
- **Which law:** Barnes says the law banned blasphemy, which is how they saw the title. Ellicott points to Leviticus 24:16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-7.htm
- Calvin says they claimed to be acting lawfully, not from hatred, because they felt Pilate's rebuke. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol35/htm/ix.ii.htm

**v. 8 (Pilate "even more afraid")**
- **What he feared:** Benson suggests Pilate suspected Jesus might be divine, having heard about his miracles. Barnes says John doesn't give the reason but probably it was a troubled conscience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-8.htm
- One commentator mentions the warning from Pilate's wife and Pilate wondering whether he had flogged a messenger of the gods. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-1.htm
- Guzik cites Tasker that it may mean "exceedingly afraid." He notes that Romans knew stories of gods appearing in human form. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/john/john-19.cfm
- The Bridgeway commentary on StudyLight says Pilate wondered if Jesus was one of the gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-7.html

**v. 9**
- Chuck Smith explains the trips indoors and out: the Jewish leaders wouldn't enter the hall during the feast. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Jhn/Jhn_129.cfm
- I found no comment on Jesus' silence.

**v. 10**
- Precept Austin: Pilate boasts of his authority just after handing that authority to the mob. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-19-commentary

**v. 11 ("given from above"; "greater sin")**
- **Authority comes from God:** GotQuestions links this to Romans 13:1. Jesus submitted to Pilate out of obedience to the Father, not because Pilate was greater. https://www.gotquestions.org/greater-sin.html
- One commentator says Pilate's power was legitimate because it came from God, so he was bound to use it justly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-1.htm
- **Who "handed me over":**
  - Caiaphas: GotQuestions; Ellicott (who rules out Judas, because Judas handed Jesus to the Jews, not to Pilate); Bengel and Meyer, per the Pulpit Commentary. https://www.gotquestions.org/greater-sin.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-11.htm
  - The Sanhedrin and people as a whole: Godet, per the Pulpit Commentary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-11.htm
  - Judas, the priests and the council together: Barnes and Gill. Clarke includes Judas as well. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-11.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-11.html
- **Why the sin was greater:** Most say it was because they acted with more knowledge and out of malice (Gill, Poole, JFB). Barnes and the Expositor's Greek Testament add that they misused a God-given office to carry out their scheme. Constable says Caiaphas abused a greater, priestly trust. Most note that Pilate still sinned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-11.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-11.html
- **Degrees of sin (Reformed):** Ligonier and The Gospel Coalition use this verse to teach that some sins are greater than others, tied to how much a person knew of God's revelation. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/degrees-sin ; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/degrees-of-sin/ GotQuestions also sees God's control and human guilt together here (compare Acts 2:23). https://www.gotquestions.org/greater-sin.html

**v. 12 ("no friend of Caesar")**
- **Pilate's fear:** One commentary on the v. 8 page says Pilate dreaded being reported to the emperor Tiberius, who was known for suspicion and harsh punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-8.htm
- Matthew Henry notes Jesus had refused earthly kingdoms. He says religion's enemies have always painted it as a danger to rulers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_019.cfm
- Bridgeway says the leaders warned that Pilate himself would be in danger if he freed a traitor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-7.html

**v. 13**
- Barclay mentions, as a possibility only, that Pilate seated Jesus himself on the judgment seat as a final mocking gesture. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dsb/john-19.html
- I found nothing else on Gabbatha.

**v. 14 (Preparation Day; "the sixth hour")**
- **Clash with Mark 15:25 ("the third hour," about 9 a.m.):** Ellicott says no solution is wholly satisfactory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-14.htm
- **Proposed solutions:**
  - **Roman clock (counting from midnight, so about 6 a.m.):** Coffman (labelled Restoration Movement and Arminian on StudyLight) and Matthew Henry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-14.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/15-25.html Bible Hub's Q&A pages lean this way too. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_the_sixth_hour_important_in_John_19_14.htm
  - **Three-hour blocks of the day:** Gill, following Lightfoot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-14.htm
  - **A copying error, with "third" as the original:** JFB and Clarke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-14.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/15-25.html
  - **Leave the difference and prefer John, who stood at the cross:** Meyer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-14.htm
  - **Rough timekeeping without clocks:** GotQuestions also mentions this. https://www.gotquestions.org/what-time-was-Jesus-crucified.html
- **Catholic voice:** Lapide calls Augustine's solution "violent," meaning forced. He reports Ribera's view that Pilate gave in at the third hour and formally sentenced at the sixth. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wyc/john/19-14.html
- **Passover lamb meaning:** GotQuestions mentions the idea that noon was when the Passover lamb was chosen, though it doubts the timing fits. https://www.gotquestions.org/what-time-was-Jesus-crucified.html Bible Hub's Q&A says that either way, the Lamb of God stands condemned while the Passover lambs are being prepared. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_the_sixth_hour_important_in_John_19_14.htm
- **"Here is your King!":** JFB calls it Pilate's ironic revenge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-14.htm

**v. 15 ("We have no king but Caesar")**
- **Most see it as giving up God's rule over Israel and the hope of the Messiah:**
  - Ellicott: it denies their own highest hopes. Vincent calls it "the formal abdication of the Messianic hope." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-15.htm
  - Gill says it contradicts their own prayer "we have no king but God" and admits that the right to rule had left Judah (Genesis 49:10), citing Hosea 3:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-15.htm
  - Calvin calls it madness that cut them off from God's grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-15.html
- **Hypocrisy:** The leaders hated Caesar. https://biblehub.com/study/john/19-15.htm
- **Judgment:** JFB (quoting Alford), Coffman and Matthew Henry link it to Rome destroying Jerusalem in AD 70. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-15.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_019.cfm
- **Pressure on Pilate:** Smith reads it as an implied threat to report him to Caesar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/19-15.html

**v. 19 (the title on the cross)**
- **Pilate's role:** Bible.org and the Expositor's Greek Testament say Pilate had it written, choosing the exact words to insult the Jews. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-19 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-19.htm
- **Each Gospel gives the wording slightly differently.** B. W. Johnson suggests the three languages explain the variations. https://ccel.org/ccel/johnson_bw/john/john.john19.iii.html
- **Christ proclaimed King:** The Geneva note says Christ, enthroned on the cross, is proclaimed everlasting King of all by the very man who condemned him for claiming a kingdom. Gill draws meaning from the name "Jesus" (Saviour). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-19.htm
- **The two charges linked:** One commentator says the priests' charge (blasphemy) and Pilate's charge (rebellion) go together: if he is the Son of God, he is the King. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-19.htm

**v. 20 (three languages)**
- JFB: Hebrew or Aramaic was the local language, Greek the common one, and Latin the official one, so every onlooker could read it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-19.htm
- Benson sees God's hand in the cross carrying the languages of peoples soon to be won to the faith. Another commentator calls it a sign of Israel's humiliation, and notes that a Jew would have written "King of Israel." Same URL.

**v. 21**
- Benson: the priests hated it because it implied he had been recognised as Messiah. JFB: they wanted it to state a false claim rather than his true dignity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-19.htm
- B. W. Johnson: Pilate meant the sign to sting the priests. https://ccel.org/ccel/johnson_bw/john/john.john19.iii.html
